segments.text: Follow the two architectures from input to digest.
Oxide's quartz core receives one byte per clock through the local adapter.
Those bytes fill two block buffers, each 136 bytes wide.
One buffer fills while the other feeds the Kekak state.
After 24 permutation rounds, the result is copied into a separate digest register.
Double buffering keeps the byte stream input moving.
Now, keep that reference above and look at the changes below.
The compact core accepts the full 8-byte DMA beat into a small buffer.
An aligned exclusive OR feeds it directly into the hash state.
The two full block buffers are gone.
The digest also reads directly from the held state, removing another register.
The outlined blocks show where storage and input logic changed.
Capture and absorption still use separate cycles.
The 24-round permutation is unchanged.
There are two more refinements inside the compact core.
Compared with the earlier wide version,
padding uses static decoding in the 17-rate lanes,
instead of selecting across all 25 state lanes.
Framing checks are registered before they control state updates.
These changes reduce surrounding logic
without changing the simulated cycle count.
The separate standalone synthesis comparison
drops from 5,664 lookup tables to 4,498.
Now, run both SHA-3 256 cores from the same dashboard.
Check the board, choose the 16.8 MB sample, and enable the core comparison.
One file, two implementations.
The file travels over USB and is verified in the board's memory.
Those transfer seconds are outside the hash timer.
The dashboard loads Oxide's Quartz Core first, then the Compact Core.
Each gets a warm-up and seven measured runs through the same local API.
Here are the two results, side by side. Oxide's time is on the left, the compact core's time is on the right.
The file is identical, and both hardware digests match the independent PC reference.
That is the architecture change made visible. Less input storage and less time hashing this large file.
